Life Stages. The age-graded periods that human development passes through, each characterized by distinctive biological, psychological, and social challenges and achievements. From infancy through old age, individuals confront predictable developmental tasks—establishing autonomy, forming identity, building relationships, pursuing achievement, and integrating life experience. Life-stage frameworks help psychologists and educators understand development as a structured process rather than a simple progression of years.

Erik Erikson proposed eight psychosocial stages spanning infancy to old age. Each is defined by a central conflict between opposing impulses. Trust versus mistrust marks infancy. Autonomy versus shame appears in toddlerhood. Childhood is marked by rapid physical growth, emerging autonomy, and socialization into cultural roles. The period involves dependency on caregivers and vulnerability to attachment disruption. Adolescence involves puberty, identity formation, and peer orientation. The period is characterized by questioning authority, experimenting with roles, and shifting from parental dependence to peer interdependence.

Early adulthood centers on autonomy, career establishment, and intimate relationships. Tasks include choosing occupation, forming partnerships, and establishing independence from family of origin. Middle adulthood often involves mentoring younger generations, maintaining relationships and careers, and confronting mortality. This generative phase may involve midlife reassessment and renewed purpose. Late adulthood brings integration of life experience and confrontation with mortality. Successful aging involves reflecting on accomplishments, maintaining relationships and activities, and finding meaning in retrospect. Continuity theory suggests that personality and coping styles remain relatively stable across life stages. People continue engaging in familiar activities and roles even as bodies and social circumstances change.

Each life stage presents distinctive developmental tasks. Infants must form secure attachments. Adolescents must establish identity. Middle-aged adults often confront questions of legacy and meaning. Older adults work toward ego integrity and acceptance. Erik Erikson was the psychologist who developed the influential eight-stage life-development model. Psychosocial development is the theoretical framework organizing development by age-related psychological and social challenges. Developmental psychology is the discipline studying age-related psychological change. Identity formation is the central psychological task of adolescence and early adulthood. Childhood is the earliest life stage characterized by dependence and rapid development. Adolescence is the life stage spanning puberty and identity exploration. Attachment theory is the framework explaining emotional bonds forming in early life stages.
